items.body_text:
Pictured: 'Kind and caring' man, 32, killed in Tube station attack while on his way home from Notting Hill Carnival - as family pay tribute to fiancé who was getting married next year
- See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
The devastated family of a 'kind and caring' man who was killed on his way home from the Notting Hill Carnival today revealed he was about to marry his fiancée.
Thomas Jewitt, who worked in affordable housing, was set upon and suffered serious head injuries on the Central Line platform at Liverpool Street station over the August bank holiday weekend.
The 32-year-old, who had attended the Notting Hill Carnival's family day, was taken to hospital in a critical condition but died three days later.
His family today expressed their disbelief that he had been 'taken from us' earlier this month, releasing a picture of him smiling on holiday.
They were at his bedside when he passed away, just months before he was due to marry.
'We can't believe that Tom has been taken from us. Tom was fun-loving, caring and kind. He always looked out for others and made them feel better,' his family said in a statement.
'He had a successful career in affordable housing, and a bright future that was taken away from him too soon. He was excited about marrying his fiancée next year.
'Tom is deeply loved by his family, his many, many friends and his work colleagues. We will draw what strength we can from the wonderful memories we have of Tom.'
British national Jeremiah Maximo, 38, of Barking, was previously charged with grievous bodily harm on September 1 and was due to appear at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court.
Following Mr Jewitt's death, British Transport Police said they would apply to amend the charge, with the defendant now expected to appear in court at a later date.
His GBH charge could now be amended to one of murder or manslaughter.
Thomas Jewitt was taken to hospital in a critical condition but died three days later
Thomas was assaulted at Liverpool Street Station (pictured) while making his way home from Notting Hill Carnival
Police rushed to reports of a 'serious assault' at Liverpool Street station's Central Line platform at 10.51pm on Sunday, August 30.
It is thought Tom attended the west London carnival's 'family day' and he had been making his way from the event when he was attacked.
The August Bank Holiday weekend marked the 60th anniversary of Notting Hill Carnival, with between one and two million revellers thought to have attended the event.
BTP Detective Superintendent Sam Blackburn said: 'First and foremost our thoughts are firmly with the loved ones of the young man who has sadly died. They are being supported by specially trained officers as our investigation continues.
'We continue to appeal to anyone who saw what happened and has not yet spoken to police to come forward and assist our investigation. Any piece of information could be vital to us.'
In a previous statement, Mr Blackburn said: 'We know the victim was travelling back from Notting Hill Carnival at the time of the incident.'
Notting Hill Carnival saw a record 636 arrests in 2026 as the number of people detained increased for the fourth consecutive year.
A total of 242 arrests took place at the festival in west London on the Sunday and 394 on the Saturday - with offences ranging from possession of drugs and weapons to assaults, including attacks on emergency workers and sexual offences.
The 636 arrests across the two-day event were up from 528 last year, and 334 the year before that.
Live facial recognition technology resulted in 121 arrests and 86 registered sex offenders being stopped.
Seven of the sex offenders were found to be breaching their conditions and were arrested.
Stop and search resulted in 68 weapons, including a handgun, being found. There were two assaults with knives, one stabbing and one slashing, neither of which resulted in life-threatening injuries.

Royal family live: Earl Spencer’s claims about Charles branded ‘utter nonsense’ after Prince Harry dodges row
Royal insiders told the Mirror that King Charles is being treated as ‘a punching bag’ in order to publicise the explosive book penned by Princess Diana’s brother Earl Spencer
Royal sources have hit back at astonishing claims made by Earl Spencer in his new book, calling the accusations ‘utter nonsense’. Princess Diana’s brother has penned a memoir about his late sister’s life and tragic death sparking a furious war of words with Buckingham Palace.
In the first excerpts from the book, Spencer has claimed that Charles was ‘giddily elated’ when he heard of Diana’s death, as well as reportedly saying in the days after her passing that the world would ‘forget about her soon enough’.
Royal sources have expressed their dismay at the monarch being treated as a ‘punching bag’ in order to publicise the explosive book.
One source, who worked for the royal family for a decade said: “(The allegations) couldn't be further from the truth of a man (King Charles) who was deeply affected by Diana’s death.”
The source added: “To claim anything other than he was overwhelmingly concerned for the wellbeing of his sons’ futures, without their mother, is simply contumelious.”
Key Events
King Charles carries out engagement after latest Earl Spencer revelations
The monarch has presented the King's Medal for Music to Sir James MacMillan at Dumfries House in Scotland today.
Sir James was accompanied by his wife Lady MacMillan for the private presentation.
Sir James is a Scottish classical composer and conductor, who is known for combining modern orchestral techniques with his Scottish heritage and Catholic faith.
EXCLUSIVE: Earl Spencer's claims about King Charles dismissed as 'utter nonsense'
Earl Spencer’s explosive claims concerning King Charles’s reactions to Princess Diana’s tragic death are “utter nonsense”, according to royal sources.
Well-placed palace insiders reacted with dismay that Diana’s brother has chosen to use the monarch as “a punching bag” to publicise his tell-all memoir on his sister’s life, ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death next year.
The Earl, who has rarely spoken of Diana’s experience as part of the royal family, this week claimed he engaged in a furious row with the then Prince Charles in the days after the princess’s death and told him: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough”.
It sparked a stern rebuke from Buckingham Palace, which said in a statement: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."
One source, who worked for the royal family for a decade said: “(The allegations) couldn't be further from the truth of a man (King Charles) who was deeply affected by Diana’s death.”
The source added: “To claim anything other than he was overwhelmingly concerned for the wellbeing of his sons’ futures, without their mother, is simply contumelious.”
Another former close aide to the King, who worked alongside him as Prince of Wales, said he didn’t recognize “the way the King is being characterized in those remarks”.
Julian Payne, the monarch’s former communications secretary, told BBC Radio 4’s Today program this week that even years after Diana’s death, Charles told staffers that they must never criticize her and that her memory must be respected - a point he was “absolutely emphatic”.
In the second part of his book serialisation in a national newspaper, Spencer claimed Charles was “giddily elated” in the immediate aftermath of Diana’s death and sounded “like a lottery winner” when he spoke to him in the hours after the 1997 tragedy.
Buckingham Palace refused to comment on the latest dramatic allegations, but a source close to the King said: “The palace’s original statement speaks for itself.”

items.title: Aryna Sabalenka labelled 'salty' as decision reached on US Open final outburst after fine
items.summary: Aryna Sabalenka was hit with a fine after her on‑court behaviour boiled over during the US Open final against Elena Rybakina
items.body_text:
Aryna Sabalenka labelled 'salty' as decision reached on US Open final outburst after fine
Aryna Sabalenka was hit with a fine after her on‑court behaviour boiled over during the US Open final against Elena Rybakina
Andy Roddick has sided with Aryna Sabalenka's 'salty' US Open outbursts, while acknowledging the runner‑up has been disrespected by opponents in the past. The Belarusian received an early code violation for ball abuse, smashed her racket in frustration and later told a TV cameraman to 'f*** off' as the lens zoomed in on her post‑match defeat to Elena Rybakina.
Her conduct earned an additional £5,569 ($7,500) fine, on top of the heavy tax hit already applied to her £2million ($2.8m) runner‑up prize. A 37 per cent federal deduction and a further 9.65 per cent New York state tax reduce her take‑home to just under £1m ($1.261m). Sabalenka is one of 18 players sanctioned this year, with total fines reaching £83,520 ($112,500).
Grand Slam rules state that the maximum fine for smashing a racket is $50,000 (£37,100), although the penalties are usually a lot less. Players can also be fined anywhere between $3,000 (£2,200) and $5,000 (£3,700) for an audible obscenity.
The fines covered audible obscenities, dress code breaches and expected performance standards.
The new world No. 2 was defeated in three sets by Rybakina in New York, with Sabalenka unravelling publicly in the closing stages of the contest.
Despite the fine and the backlash from fans, Roddick insisted Sabalenka did nothing wrong. The former world No.1, who sympathised with her situation, defended her on his 'Served' podcast. "People are often looking for a reason to just be upset about something and to go Twitter finger their account," he said.
"I just think that they are going to look for something. I am not going to get mad at you if you break your own stuff. I don't care as long as you are gracious. Could she do it after? Yeah, sure.
"Am I going to be personally offended that she broke her own thing? No. She has been salty in defeat before. But I do think there is a double standard.
"If someone walks off after losing the NBA Finals, they get criticised, saying they are too happy, or they are dapping up the people they lost to. No, it's like 'they broke stuff.'
JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page
Roddick continued: "It's like, what do you want? It's like whatever, just let people live. The mistake she has made before is being disrespectful and taking credit away from your opponent in a public fashion, but I don't care what you say to your team.
"As long as there is a base level of respect for who you have played and what you have done and what they've done, if you break a racket, who cares?
"I can't imagine being an adult seeing that and then going to a social media account and being like 'I can't believe she broke a racket.' Come on, what are we doing!"
Speaking about her reaction, the 28-year-old said: "It’s really tough to control your emotions when you lose in the final of a Grand Slam and when you were trying to go for the three-peat.
"So, I just wanted to let it go because if I would hold it inside right now over here or over there on the court, I wouldn’t be able to say a word or I would just go not really nice over there. So, I just wanted to let all of that aggression and disappointment go outside."

items.title: Keely Hodgkinson shares strange MRI scan results with 'abnormal' issue found
items.summary: Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson has admitted to dealing with an unusual injury issue
items.body_text:
Keely Hodgkinson shares strange MRI scan results with 'abnormal' issue found
Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson has admitted to dealing with an unusual injury issue
Keely Hodgkinson has revealed that MRI results show she is competing with an abnormal hamstring. The 800m star is set to end her season at Athlos on Friday.
The Olympic champion started her campaign in impressive fashion, setting a new indoor world record and later claiming the World Indoor Championship title in March. More recently, her season has been defined by second-place finishes to rival Audrey Werro at the European Championships and World Ultimate Championship.
The 24-year-old has refused to make excuses for her losses to Werro but has admitted to suffering a hamstring tear when battling for the European title in Birmingham. The injury occurred just a month after Hodgkinson sustained deep cuts to her knees and jarred her back due to a freak fall in Manchester.
While the latter may have contributed to her hamstring issue, Hodgkinson was still able to make it to the start line for both of her recent duels with Werro. Her quick recovery time was aided by the Team GB star’s hamstring abnormality, which has allowed her to continue competing.
JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page
“My body’s quite literally built differently,” Hodgkinson told The Telegraph. “I have two tendons… where everyone has one tendon. We’re trying to figure out if it’s a strength or a weakness as, when one of them tears, I still have another one because it’s split. It means that you don’t feel the injury until later on when it gets a bit tight.”
Reflecting on her injury during the European Championships, Hodgkinson said: “I was like, ‘Oh, something’s not quite right’ but it didn’t affect me during the race.”
The injury setbacks have contributed to Hodgkinson’s mixed fortunes on the track. However, her unusual hamstring can also work in the British icon’s favour after the issue was identified in 2025.
“Yeah, it’s just how I’m made. We found that on an MRI scan last year when I tore it,” she explained. “As a pro, it means that when one is down, I can still run on the one that works. As a con, maybe it’s slightly weaker than the one that’s [normally] attached.
“You can still run on them. So I haven’t missed any training, I’ve just had to alter my approach. I’ve had to take my foot off the speed, because that’s when it’s most risky. But my body heals very, very well, so I couldn’t really feel anything.”
Having claimed the indoor record earlier this season, Hodgkinson had set her sights on eclipsing the overall record of 1:53.28, which has been held by Jarmila Kratochvilova since 1983. Hodgkinson’s personal best currently stands at 1:54.33, while her rival Werro ran 1:53.70 earlier this year.
“I wanted to get this world record. I’m good, but I need someone to help me push to these times,” Hodgkinson said. “It’s too difficult on your own. Audrey’s done incredible this year. I think we will get that eventually. I hope everyone’s enjoyed watching. I’ve still enjoyed competing even though it’s not quite been the season I wanted.”
She is set to sign off for the season at Athlos on Friday, an all-women’s event being held in Barnet. Defending champion Hodgkinson could earn £48,000 ($65,000) for winning the 800m event, while series champions will receive an extra £18,000 ($25,000) and a Tiffany & Co. crown.

items.title: Putin will have Trump to thank for election victory in Russia’s rubber-stamp parliament
items.summary: Sam Kiley, world affairs editor, explains the significance of the insignificant Russian Duma elections
items.body_text:
Russians go to the polls in elections to its parliament amid a fuel crisis, mortuaries swollen with war dead, and an economy that is shrinking. All ingredients point to what should be a landslide against the ruling United Russia Party.
But when the results are announced towards the end of this month, Vladimir Putin’s rubber-stamp-representatives are certain to emerge victorious. They are likely to have the 300+ seats in the Duma to rewrite the constitution.
Putin will have the US president to thank for that. Donald Trump has hamstrung Ukraine by cutting military aid, taken Russia’s side in all negotiations for peace, inexplicably ignored Russia’s support for Iran it the war he started against Tehran, and is now sitting on legislation that would cut back on Putin’s profits from oil price spikes that Trump caused.
Russia’s president is so powerful that he isn’t even a member of the United Russia Party. And to make sure there’s no place for opposition in a new Duma, where dissident voices could be heard and ignored, independent candidates have been squeezed out of registration well ahead of the polls.
Boris Nadezhdin launched a campaign in 2024 on an anti-war platform and even gained the 100,000 signatures he needed to run for the Duma. He was then declared a ‘foreign agent” and forbidden to collect the signatures he already had.
He was soon detained and fined for posting a photograph of Alexei Navalny, the opposition leader poisoned in a Kremlin jail and then banned from leaving Russia.
His natural response was to finally say: “I am not willing to put at risk those who support me and took part in the election campaign — my family, my campaign team, the signature collectors and my supporters.” He fled Russia and now lives in exile.
The independent Russian pollsters the Levada Center's August survey found 76% approved of Putin's performance and 18% disapproving. Some 56% said Russia was moving in the right direction versus 27% saying it was on the wrong course.
Polling under a violent dictatorship that that has invaded a neighbour should be seen as skewing for personal safety – telling the truth on the threshold of your home could lead to a fatal tumble off a balcony in the same flat.
Still, recent polling found that Russians are now feeling some of the pain of the country’s war against Ukraine. Kyiv has been launching effective long ranger missile attacks and hitting closer to 50 per cent of Russia’s oil refining sites.
Levada found that 55% said petrol shortages had made their lives more difficult, with 32% saying they had seriously complicated life. Dissatisfaction was markedly higher among poorer Russians, younger people and those already critical of Putin.
Putin’s approval rating has dipped below 80 per cent for the first time since he ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine – by only about 8 per cent though. There may be erosion of support for Putin but not a collapse.
Growth has stalled to roughly 1–1.3% for 2026 after a wartime spending boom pushed it above 4% in 2023–24, and the economy has effectively split in two.
There is a state-subsidized military-industrial sector that’s expanding, and a civilian economy — small and medium enterprises especially — stagnating or shrinking.
Putin has used the National Wealth Fund, Russia's sovereign reserve, to fund his war. But it’s a thinning cushion. It held $113.5 billion in liquid assets before the 2022 invasion. Now it’s got $50 billion, or less.
The Israeli-US war against Iran caused oil prices spikes that delivered a bonanza for Russia at a time when Ukraine has trying to drive the Kremlin out of the war by killing so many Russians that Moscow could no longer afford the $165,000 compensation for those killed in action.
Oil price hikes have meant a daily bonus worth up to $150 million a day, according to Chatham House.
A bill that’s been passed by both the US houses is now sitting on Trump’s desk.

items.title: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman after 56 years
items.summary: Warren Buffett has been at the company for over 60 years, and served as chairman since 1970
items.body_text:
Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman after 56 years
Warren Buffett has been at the company for over 60 years, and served as chairman since 1970
- Bookmark
Warren Buffett is standing down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway after leading the conglomerate for more than 50 years.
Buffett, 96, will assume the role of chairman emeritus immediately, the company announced on Friday. His son, Howard, who has sat on the Berkshire Hathaway board since 1993, will become the new chairman as part of a long-planned succession.
Warren Buffett will remain a director, having served as chairman of the company since 1970.
Greg Abel took over for Buffett as the CEO of the $1 trillion conglomerate to start the year, but Buffett remains one of the most influential investors in the world.
"I have served Berkshire since 1965," Buffett said in a letter to shareholders. "Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world. That is not something many people my age can say, and I have never felt better about what comes next."
Buffett expressed his full confidence in Abel and his son Howard to lead Berkshire Hathaway forward.
"Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet," he said. "Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against."
The vast majority of Buffett's fortune has been amassed through Berkshire Hathaway stock, reaching a valuation of more than $140 billion in July 2026.
He has already given away roughly $66 billion worth of stock since 2006.
Over the years, Buffett has cultivated a devoted following, and when Berkshire Hathaway reveals the stocks that the company has acquired or sold in public disclosures, it can shake markets.
During his tenure as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, the company nearly doubled the returns of the S&P 500, with a 19.9 per cent compounded annual growth rate compared with the index’s 10.4 per cent gain.
"Warren’s impact on Berkshire and its owners is without parallel in the history of American business," Abel said in a prepared statement. "The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian."

items.title: Sydney woman who killed and dismembered abusive husband could be eligible for parole in a year
items.summary: Nirmeen Noufl, 55, pleaded guilty last month to killing her husband in self-defence
items.body_text:
Sydney woman who killed and dismembered abusive husband could be eligible for parole in a year
Nirmeen Noufl, 55, pleaded guilty last month to killing her husband in self-defence
- Bookmark
A Sydney woman who killed and dismembered her abusive husband was sentenced on Friday to three years in jail, with a further year added for disposing of the body.
Nirmeen Noufl, 55, pleaded guilty last month to killing Mamdouh Noufl, 62. She had acted to defend herself, she claimed, but used more force than the law allowed. Her husband was reported missing in July 2023 and his body was never found.
Noufl was arrested in October 2024 after police searched the couple’s home in Greenacre in southwest Sydney.
Since Noufl had been in custody since her arrest, Justice Peter Hamill ruled, she would be eligible for parole in October next year.
In the course of the trial, prosecution and defence lawyers agreed on the account of what transpired: the couple had an argument one night in May 2023 which turned physical. Noufl told psychiatrists she was pinned to the kitchen floor and choked when she reached for a renovation tool and stabbed her husband, "believing that her life was in danger”.
The judge said he was not satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that she had intended to kill her husband.
Noufl then dismembered the body. A witness who was at the house in the following days told the court they saw “pieces of a large round saw” which had been dismantled, alongside fragments of plastic, some with blood on them.
The dismembered body was put in garbage bags and dumped in bins with the help of that witness, who could not be identified for legal reasons. Justice Hamill said the disposal of the body was a "disturbing" feature of the case.
"The disposal of the body in this case was as thorough as it was brutal," he said.
"The conduct after the killing is remarkable and chilling, and is relevant to issues such as remorse, rehabilitation and future dangerousness."
The judge said Noufl's history of childhood dysfunction and domestic violence was relevant to her sentence.
The account agreed by both sides stated that the marriage had been marred by infidelity and domestic violence, much of it unreported. Mamdouh Noufl is described in court documents as strict, controlling, and holding conservative Islamic views.
He had met a woman during a 2022 trip to Egypt, where the couple owned property, and declared that he planned to marry her but refused Noufl's request for divorce.
Noufl was reported as telling another witness after her husband's death that he had "treated me like s***" and that she had "had enough”.
The court also heard evidence from the couple's children, who described the relationship as "gravely abusive”, featuring violence, manipulation and coercive control.
Mamdouh Noufl's relatives, including his siblings, niece and nephew, gave statements describing his positive qualities.
His brother called him kind, respectable, friendly and compassionate, and relatives said that the dismemberment amounted to "horrific cruelty", leaving no resting place to visit.
"Look what she did to him,” one of his nephews said angrily outside the court. “If it was an accident, if she was not meant to kill him, why did you f****** dismember his body?"
Noufl's defence lawyer, Mohamed Bejjaoui, described the case as "a tragic set of circumstances" that had been "difficult on everybody, especially the family”.
He said his client planned to live with her children after her release and hoped the family could move on.
Asked whether Noufl was remorseful, he said: "She is, she is. Definitely."

items.title: Inside West Ham’s power struggle as ‘Trump-like’ Sullivan lingers
items.summary: The 77-year-old ‘isn’t going anywhere’ after a recent shareholding increase
items.body_text:
Ahead of West Ham United’s first visit to Millwall since 2011, the news that David Sullivan will not be in attendance at The Den appears somewhat ironic.
The West Ham shareholder and controversial former vice-chairman, who resigned from his key role and directorship at the club in June amid allegations of misconduct, has already ignored requests to stay away from home games at the London Stadium this season.
His presence at the Charlton Athletic fixture last month was described as “deliberately provocative” by the West Ham Fan Advisory Board, with Sullivan then in attendance for matches against Wolverhampton Wanderers, Derby County and Wrexham as well.
It comes as the 77-year-old has seen his shareholding in West Ham increase from 38.8 to 40 per cent as a consequence of Daniel Kretinsky taking advantage of pre-emptive share rights to firm up his post as majority shareholder.
The shift in the Hammers’ ownership has thwarted recent attempts by businesswoman and former Newcastle United co-owner Amanda Staveley to obtain a 25.1 per cent stake in the club after a binding agreement was reached in August with Vanessa Gold, the club’s joint-chair.
West Ham’s existing board members subsequently blocked the deal by triggering their contractual “pre-emption rights” (right of first refusal).
From an on-field perspective, West Ham are on a four-game winning streak in their quest for a return to the Premier League following relegation to the second tier last season.
Nuno Espírito Santo’s side – favourites to win the Championship – are top of the table on goal difference prior to the eagerly anticipated clash at Millwall, where absence has not made mutual hearts grow fonder on either side of the Thames.
Has the positivity on the pitch tempered some of the anger at Sullivan’s seemingly intractable position, with supporters keen on a fresh start at ownership level?
At one point, it appeared Staveley, husband Mehrdad Ghodoussi, and their vehicle PCP Capital Partners would become involved and potentially contribute to significant structural changes around the London Stadium. However, such a development appears to be in the east London long grass for now.
“I think if David Sullivan was going to leave he would have done so by now,” a club source told The i Paper.
“After everything that has gone on over the last few months and beyond, you might have thought that would be the case. But he tends to come along (to games) and simply has the air of someone who couldn’t care less what supporters think of him.
“You don’t get to where he is without making a few enemies along the way. There’s nothing new about that in business, but when you are a high-profile figure of a big football club where the fans, by and large, want you out, then it becomes an ongoing problem that can only be solved with Sullivan leaving.
“Sullivan knows all about his unpopularity – how could you not? This is someone, remember, who attends the London Stadium even when police and Newham council strongly recommended that he doesn’t, due to the potential of disorder.”
Despite supporters marching in their thousands from Stratford station to London Stadium last November, Sullivan remains unmoved.
“It’s almost as if he (Sullivan) regards himself as a Trump-like figure,” the source added.
“Completely self-satisfied and immune to everyone and all the public criticism around him. Yes, he has resigned from the board but he now has 40 per cent of the club shareholding, so in that sense it looks like, for the moment, he isn’t going anywhere.”
Kretinsky, owner of Royal Mail, has made all the right noises in relation to West Ham’s governance after Staveley’s consortium was denied a stake. The Czech businessman has been criticised by fans for his lack of regular visits to London Stadium.

items.title: 11 things to look for when choosing a secondary school, according to headteachers
items.summary: Speak to as many children as possible when visiting a school. If there aren't many current pupils attending an open day, that could be a red flag
items.body_text:
Close to three quarters of a million children begin their final year in primary school this month. Across the country, schools are holding open events now to help parents decide where to apply by the deadline of 31 October (and parents like me, with children in Year 5, are already looking ahead).
As a place where teenagers spend much of their time – up to 70 per cent – for five or seven years, parents’ choice of a secondary school can have a huge impact on the next stage of their children’s lives. If you’re lucky enough to have a choice of suitable schools in your area, it’s important to make the most of any access.
As the prospective parent of a Year 7 student for the first time, I’m keen to use any time on school grounds wisely – and asked parents and headteachers for advice on how to make the most of a visit.
Shorts
Look beyond reputation
Sean Maher, headteacher at Richard Challoner School, an all-boys Catholic secondary in Kingston, London, says the very best thing to take to an open event is an open mind. “Some places will have historic reputations, but you shouldn’t listen to what your hairdresser or someone who went there years ago says,” he advises. “Personal recommendations are best.” And be cautious of thinking that private schools are better than state schools. “Some private schools are fantastic but some really aren’t value for money.”
Put the child first, not yourself
Mark Pain is headteacher of the Charter School North Dulwich, one of the country’s top performing non-selective schools, though he admits it is selective in that the area is affluent and people buy houses there for proximity to his school. He has children in Year 6 himself at the moment. His top piece of advice is to consider their needs as much, if not more, than your own. “Make sure it’s about what your child wants as opposed to what you want. One of the things I do [at his own school’s open events] is deliberately talk to the children rather than the parents.”
“I think it’s as much their decision as yours. As parents we can get carried away thinking, ‘This is the right school as they get amazing academic outcomes or they do this sport and that sport.’”
Happiness, mental health and pastoral care are vital
So what does matter to children? “It’s more about whether the student’s going to be happy, and about making sure they have a sense of belonging,” he says. “Parents should look out for whether the staff are engaging with children as well as with them.”
Jo MacDonald, founder of Creative Counselling Margate, is also looking at secondary schools for the first time. “As a parent, I know how hard it is to set aside your own assumptions and ambitions,” she says. “But as a therapist, I know the real question isn’t which school looks right to me, but which one feels right to them. I’ll always ask about the behaviour policy – it tells you more about a school’s soul than any league table. And you won’t be surprised to hear that I’ll check whether there’s a counsellor on-site, and how easily an anxious eleven-year-old could actually find them. In the end, the best school isn’t the one you’d choose for your child, it’s the one you helped your child choose for themselves.”
Do your homework
Neil Renton is the headteacher of Harrogate Grammar School, a large secondary school and a grammar only in name. He suggests that parents do as much research as possible before any open event to get a feel for whether the school is a good fit for them and their child. “Look at the social media, website and how the school communicates,” he says. “Does this fit with you as a parent?”
Look at the Progress 8 score
Choosing a school based on its academic results is something that I struggle with. It’s easy to have one’s head turned by a bevvy of starred grades, but deep down I know they’re no marker for a life well-lived. items.title: Our kids think their dad Rob Beckett is the fun one. Guess who makes it possible?
items.summary: Lou Beckett: It’s hard to compete with someone who looks like a cartoon come to life
items.body_text:
Daddy’s the fun one. Of course he is. Look at him. It’s hard to compete with someone who looks like a cartoon come to life. He’s also 20 years into a career where his sole mission has been to make people laugh. That’s what he’s programmed for, his every fibre constantly scanning for an opportunity to turn that frown upside down – and there’s no audience he enjoys more than our girls.
I, on the other hand, spent the best part of my professional life as a secondary school history teacher, a profession not exactly renowned for being a laugh – essentially, a qualified teller-off of children. It’s not a fair fight.
Pathological need for attention aside, the girls think Rob’s more fun than I am simply because he’s not Mummy. I’m not the only mum who’s somehow found herself as chief executive of her own family, responsible for the Sisyphean task of everything, all of the time, for everyone. Which is a lot when you think about it. The mental load and disproportionate division of domestic labour mean that mums are spending significantly more time managing the family than their partners do. This doesn’t just take away from the time women have to invest in themselves, but also from the time they have to enjoy the family they’re working so hard for.
It’s easier to be fun when you’re coming at it fresh, when you’ve been set up for success by someone who’s already dealt with the boring stuff. No one wants to be “Shouty Mum”. “Shouty Mum” isn’t what I had children to be. I wanted to be “Earth Mother Mum”, “Down with the Kids Cool Mum” or even “Freshly Baked Organic Goods Mum”. “Shouty Mum” wasn’t on the 2015 vision board.
“Shouty Mum” has a recurring role in the soap opera of our life, though, because sometimes “Patient Mum”, “Asked 17 Times Before Mum” or “Overstimulated by Bickering Mum” has long since run out of patience. “Shouty Dad” isn’t really a thing in our house, probably because Rob’s worked away so much in the last few years – topping out at almost 200 nights last year alone – that his tolerance for the selective deafness or intense bickering of children hasn’t worn thin yet. He’s not on his last nerve, whereas I waved goodbye to mine long ago. If it doesn’t sound fair, it’s because it isn’t. Parenting is almost impossible to divide equally, especially if your work schedules are as mismatched as ours.
I know that one day my girls will look back and appreciate how much work I was doing that was invisible to an eight-year-old’s eye: the silent tasks and labour that most mums have assumed by default. Maybe, in the eternal cycle of parenthood, if they have their own children one day, they’ll look at me and say a thank you that’ll hit differently because they’ll have lived it themselves, the way I saw my own mum in a completely different light once I had the girls. I finally understood just how much of herself she had poured into our family, never once outwardly begrudging my dad the hero’s welcome he received when he came home from work – despite rarely receiving one herself.
I want to be the fun one, too. I don’t want to wait 20 years for my girls to realise I wasn’t not fun – I was just tired. Call me needy, but I’m a hoot and they need to know that. After a minor Damascene realisation that probably involved one of them telling me how much more fun Daddy was, I accepted that if I was feeling like a martyr to motherhood, then I needed to change something and stop assuming responsibilities that could be shared just because I was Mum.
If dads are stealing all the glory, then we’ve got to bring “Fun Mum” out to play sometimes. The girls are so used to me as “Logistics Mum”, “Homework Mum” or “School Run Mum” that the unpredictability of “Fun Mum” blows their minds. The hysteria that ensues when I go rogue is electrifying. I can see why Rob’s so desperate to make people laugh all the time: it’s a physical high.

items.title: Royan Institute achieves global milestone in regenerative medicine with WhartoCell
items.summary: TEHRAN – Iran has taken a major step forward in regenerative medicine with the approval of WhartoCell, an allogeneic stem cell therapy developed by researchers at Royan Institute to treat osteoarthritis.
items.body_text:
Royan Institute achieves global milestone in regenerative medicine with WhartoCell
TEHRAN – Iran has taken a major step forward in regenerative medicine with the approval of WhartoCell, an allogeneic stem cell therapy developed by researchers at Royan Institute to treat osteoarthritis.
The achievement was also highlighted by MedPath, an international platform specializing in medical information, clinical trials, and healthcare technologies, putting the spotlight on Royan Institute’s contribution to this scientific and technological breakthrough.
According to Mehdi Lotfipanah, Director of Public Relations and International Affairs at Royan Institute, the therapy is designed to reduce inflammation, support cartilage regeneration, and improve joint function in patients with osteoarthritis. “The introduction of innovative cell-based therapies requires a scientific and evidence-based approach to ensure their appropriate integration into clinical practice,” Lotfipanah said.
Technical Profile and Mechanism of Action
WhartoCell is derived from Wharton’s jelly of the neonatal umbilical cord, a rich source of mesenchymal stem cells. These cells possess anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties while supporting tissue repair and regeneration. A distinguishing feature of the product is that it does not require genetic matching, or human leukocyte antigen (HLA) matching, between donor and recipient.
This characteristic allows physicians to administer the treatment without lengthy preparation procedures, positioning WhartoCell as an off-the-shelf therapy expected to improve patient access to advanced regenerative treatments.
Manufacturing and Quality Standards
Royan Institute has emphasized that WhartoCell is manufactured under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, with quality and safety monitored throughout the production process. This adherence to internationally recognized manufacturing standards is intended to ensure consistent product quality and patient safety.
Broader Clinical Potential
Although WhartoCell was initially approved for osteoarthritis, researchers at Royan Institute suggest the technology may have broader applications in regenerative medicine. Potential future indications include cartilage repair, tendon and ligament injuries, bone fracture healing, avascular necrosis, and the management of inflammatory joint disorders.
Strategic Significance
Lotfipanah noted that the product represents an important achievement in developing indigenous biotechnology, reducing dependence on imported therapeutic products while expanding access for healthcare providers across the country. He added that greater awareness among physicians and healthcare providers would facilitate broader adoption of regenerative medicine technologies.
 
 Royan Institute plans to increase scientific communication around WhartoCell through specialized workshops, educational programs for physicians and patients, and scientific meetings, including activities tied to the upcoming 27th International Royan Congress. The institute, one of Iran’s leading centers for stem cell research and regenerative medicine, has developed several advanced cell-based therapeutic technologies over the past two decades as part of the country’s growing biotechnology sector.
Iran among top 10 countries in regenerative medicine
With the approval of six new advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs), Iran has showcased breakthroughs in regenerative medicine, improving the country’s global ranking from 12 to 7.
According to the latest global report, out of 148 ATMPs approved in 2025 under the supervision of 12 internationally recognized regulatory bodies, seven were made in Iran, placing it among the top 10 countries in the field, IRNA reported.
The number of licensed products in regenerative medicine has grown from one product in the Iranian year 1402 (March 2023-March 2024) to seven in Iranian year 1404 (March 2025 – March 2026.

items.title: Iranian physician wins 2025 Kuwait Prize for control of cancer
items.summary: TEHRAN – Amir-Ali Hamidieh, an Iranian professor at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, has won the State of Kuwait Prize for the Control of Cancer, Cardiovascular Diseases, and Diabetes in the Eastern Mediterranean Region.
items.body_text:
Iranian physician wins 2025 Kuwait Prize for control of cancer
TEHRAN – Amir-Ali Hamidieh, an Iranian professor at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, has won the State of Kuwait Prize for the Control of Cancer, Cardiovascular Diseases, and Diabetes in the Eastern Mediterranean Region.
The Foundation for the State of Kuwait Prize for the Control of Cancer, Cardiovascular Diseases, and Diabetes in the Eastern Mediterranean Region was established in 2003. Based on the recommendation of the Foundation Committee at its 72nd session in October 2025, the Regional Committee decided to award the Prize to Hamidieh for his significant contribution in the field of cancer.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the prize consists of a bronze medal and a sum of money; it will be presented in October during the 73rd session of the Regional Committee.
A distinguished physician, academic and pioneer in paediatric haematology, oncology and stem cell transplantation, Hamidieh earned his M.D. from Islamic Azad University, Tehran, and pursued postgraduate training in paediatrics and paediatric haematology/ oncology at Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences. He later completed advanced fellowships in haematopoietic stem cell transplantation at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center and Baylor College of Medicine in Texas, United States of America.
Hamidieh currently serves as Professor of Pediatric Hematology/ Oncology and Stem Cell Transplantation at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, where he also directs the Pediatric Cell and Gene Therapy Research Center.
He is the founder of the Iranian paediatric stem cell transplantation programme and the national stem cell donor network, which established the country’s first human leukocyte antigen (HLA) registry.
 
  
 
 He chairs the National Council for Development of Stem Cell Sciences and Technologies under the Vice-Presidency for Science and Technology and is a member of the executive boards of the Asia-Pacific Blood and Marrow Transplantation Group and the Iranian Food and Drug Administration.
His leadership has enabled the development of seven paediatric transplant centres across the Islamic Republic of Iran and the successful completion of more than 2100 paediatric stem cell transplants.
 
 Hamidieh has authored more than 100 peer-reviewed articles on research spanning regenerative medicine, gene therapy, immunodeficiencies and paediatric cancers.
He has also led clinical innovations in CAR-T cell therapy and photopheresis across many countries. Through his academic leadership, clinical excellence and commitment to equitable care, Hamidieh has significantly advanced the field of paediatric stem cell transplantation in Iran and the broader Eastern Mediterranean Region.
Majid Ghayour Mobarhan, an Iranian professor at Mashhad University of Medical Sciences, Davood Khalili, an epidemiologist and professor at the Center for Research on the Prevention of Metabolic Diseases at the Institute of Glandular Sciences at Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, Afshin Ostovar, a professor at Tehran University of Medical Science, and Fereydoun Azizi, the director of Iran’s Institute for Endocrine Sciences, won the prize in 2024, 2023, 2022, and 2007, respectively.

items.title: Iran's Guards stage show of force two days after protest anniversary
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards paraded uniformed volunteers, Basij paramilitaries and children through Tehran on Friday in a state-organized show of force, two days after the anniversary of the 2022 protests.
items.body_text:
Four years have passed since Zhina Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old woman who had travelled to Tehran to visit family, died after being detained by the morality police.
She could never have imagined how her name would appear on walls, streets and university campuses, or on the lips of millions of Iranians, or how three simple words, “Woman, Life, Freedom,” would become one of the most enduring slogans in Iran’s modern history.
The story of 2022 is not only the story of a slogan. It is the story of the price thousands paid to break through the wall of fear.
Zhina’s death on September 16, 2022, sparked protests across Iran. Human rights organizations documented live ammunition and pellet fire, mass arrests, torture, sexual violence and the killing of protesters. HRANA later recorded protests in all 31 provinces, 160 cities and 143 universities, and reported at least 530 people killed, including 68 children and teenagers.

Their stories were different, but each became part of the collective memory of Woman, Life, Freedom.
Then came the gallows. Mohammad Mehdi Karami, a 22-year-old karate champion, was executed after being sentenced in connection with the fortieth-day commemoration for Hadis Najafi. Some detainees appeared in televised “confessions” that human rights organizations said were tainted by torture. Families seeking the truth about those killed also faced pressure. Others eventually left Iran after imprisonment, threats and persecution, carrying the cost of the uprising into exile, lost careers, interrupted education and separation from family.

items.body_text:
A girl who was just entering adolescence when the Woman, Life, Freedom protests began is now approaching adulthood. The past four years have been part of the period in which her understanding of society, government and freedom has taken shape.
Women burning their headscarves, nighttime chants from apartment windows, protests in schools and universities, young people knocking turbans off clerics’ heads and protesters standing up to security forces all became part of the memories that accompanied that generation into adulthood.
One of the most enduring changes is visible on the streets.
Many women now appear without mandatory hijab in streets, universities, cafes, shopping centers and on public transport. Some ride bicycles and motorcycles without covering their hair.
The Islamic Republic has responded to this defiance with arrests and summonses, warning text messages, vehicle seizures, restrictions on bank accounts and SIM cards, surveillance cameras and the closure of businesses.
Human rights organizations say tens of thousands of women have faced security or judicial action over their clothing during the past four years.
Abandoning mandatory hijab has become one of the clearest forms of collective disobedience to emerge from 2022, continuing in parts of society despite the security and legal costs.
As the fourth anniversary of Amini’s death approached, a coalition of Iranian Kurdish political groups called for a general strike on September 16, urging people to close shops and markets and stay away from work.
From Mahsa Amini’s death to prison and executions
Mahsa “Jina” Amini, a 22-year-old woman from Saqqez in Iran’s Kordestan province was detained by the morality police in Tehran on September 13, 2022. She was taken to hospital and died three days later.
Her gravestone bears the words: “Dear Jina, you will not die. Your name will become a symbol.”
Her father, Amjad Amini, wrote on September 14, ahead of the fourth anniversary of her death, that her name had “gone beyond our small home.”
The family, he said, was still waiting for the truth to emerge.
“The sealed secret that you and all the loved ones resting in this earth carry with you will not remain hidden forever,” he wrote.
Amini’s name quickly became a rallying cry for protests that began in Saqqez and Kordestan, spread to Tehran and then swept across Iran. The Kurdish slogan “Jin, Jiyan, Azadi” and its Persian equivalent, “Woman, Life, Freedom,” became the uprising’s defining chant.
“Death to the dictator,” “This is the final message, the target is the entire system,” “Poverty, corruption, high prices — we will go on until overthrow,” and “Don’t call it a protest, it’s called a revolution” were also heard on the streets, reflecting the political direction the protests had taken.
Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and the Islamic Republic itself became the direct targets of many of the slogans.
The uprising also quickly became a global cause. Artists, athletes, academics, human rights activists and political figures around the world voiced support, carrying Amini’s name and the slogan Woman, Life, Freedom far beyond Iran’s borders.
The authorities answered the protests with lethal force, widespread injuries and mass arrests.
Human rights organizations have put the number of people killed in the uprising at more than 550. Many more were wounded, while shotgun pellets blinded dozens of protesters in one or both eyes.
Judiciary chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei said in May 2025 that more than 90,000 cases had been opened in connection with the 2022 protests, including cases involving schoolchildren, university students and teachers.
The crackdown continued in the courts after large street gatherings subsided.
Execution, imprisonment, flogging, internal exile, fines, travel bans and restrictions on social rights were among the punishments handed down to protesters and activists linked to the uprising.

یکی از مخاطبان ایراناینترنشنال که میگوید دارای معلولیت شدید و بیماری صعبالعلاج است، در پیامی از هزینه بالای دارو و قطع بیمه و یارانه خود خبر داد.
روایت شما
او گفت برای شش آمپول و سه ورق قرص دو میلیون تومان پرداخت کرده و ناچار است هفتهای چهار بار دارو تهیه کند که هزینه هر بار بین دو تا چهار میلیون تومان است.
این مخاطب افزود با وجود نداشتن درآمد، بیمه و یارانهاش به دلیل «بالا بودن تراکنشهای بانکی» قطع شده، در حالی که به گفته او این تراکنشها صرف خرید دارو میشود.
•
با وجود تعهدات بینالمللی ایران در مورد منع استفاده از کودکان در امور نظامی، اقدامات حکومت برای نظامیسازی و امنیتی کردن فضای مدارس در آستانه آغاز سال تحصیلی جدید تشدید شده است.
این اقدامات از استفاده از پلاکهای شناسایی مشابه پلاکهای جنگی تا گسترش فعالیتهای بسیج دانشآموزی در مدارس را در بر میگیرد.

همزمان، سازمان بسیج دانشآموزی که زیر نظر سپاه پاسداران انقلاب اسلامی فعالیت میکند، کارزاری با عنوان «یاوران ولایت» به اجرا گذاشته است.

این وبسایت ویدیویی از انتقال دهها موتورسیکلت در ۲۴ شهریور به پایگاه رودماهی منتشر کرد.

وزارت خزانهداری آمریکا چهارم بهمن ۱۳۹۷ لشکر فاطمیون را تحریم کرد.
فاطمیون همچنین در کنار لشکر زینبیون پاکستان و حشد شعبی عراق، نقشی کلیدی در سرکوب اعتراضات دیماه ۱۴۰۴ ایفا کرد و در هماهنگی با نیروهای نظامی جمهوری اسلامی به کشتار معترضان پرداخت.
استقرار این نیروها در سیستان و بلوچستان نگرانیهایی را در میان شهروندان درباره احتمال استفاده از آنان برای سرکوب اعتراضات ایجاد کرده است.
ادامه درگیریهای مسلحانه
استان سیستان و بلوچستان در هفتههای اخیر شاهد چندین درگیری مسلحانه میان نیروهای نظامی و امنیتی جمهوری اسلامی و گروهها و افراد مسلح بوده است.
۲۱ شهریور، درگیری حدود ۹ ساعته نیروهای حکومتی با اعضای «جبهه مبارزین مردمی» در منطقه بخشان سراوان به کشته شدن سه نیروی سپاه پاسداران و چهار فرد مسلح انجامید.
حالوش ۲۷ شهریور هویت چهار فرد کشتهشده را موسی دهواری، مبین شادزهی، محمد دهقانخلد و سلیم مزارزهی اعلام کرد.
«جبهه مبارزین مردمی» شمار تلفات نیروهای جمهوری اسلامی را ۹ کشته و ۲۱ مجروح اعلام کرد؛ آماری که از سوی منابع حکومتی تایید نشده است.
این گروه آذر ۱۴۰۴ با مشارکت شماری از گروههای فعال در سیستان و بلوچستان، از جمله «جنبش پادا بلوچ»، «حرکت نصر بلوچستان» و «جیشالعدل»، با هدف اتحاد در مبارزه تشکیل شد.
چهار سال از خیزش «زن، زندگی، آزادی» میگذرد. در این مدت، ایران شاهد تحولاتی پرشتاب و تکاندهنده بوده است؛ از جمله وقوع دو جنگ، اعتراضات دیماه و کشتار بیسابقه مردم. در میانه این تحولات، دانشگاه اکنون کجا ایستاده است و چه چشماندازی میتوان برای آینده آن متصور بود؟
تحلیل فضای دانشگاه، همچون بررسی وضعیت کلی جامعه، آسان نیست. سرعت تحولات در ایران چنان بالاست که هر لحظه ممکن است حادثهای بزرگ، معادلات موجود را تغییر دهد.
با وجود این بیثباتی و پیشبینیناپذیری، میتوان با اطمینان گفت خیزش مهسا نقطه عطفی در تاریخ معاصر ایران بود. این خیزش هیمنه جمهوری اسلامی را که بخش مهمی از آن بر کنترل بدن زنان و تحمیل حجاب اجباری استوار بوده است، در هم شکست.
پس از خیزش مهسا، فضای دانشگاهها بهشدت امنیتی شد. حکومت دیگر ابایی

items.title: US, Poland Making Progress On Permanent American Army Base, Trump Says
items.summary: US President Donald Trump says Washington and Warsaw are making "major progress" toward establishing a permanent US Army base in Poland, potentially expanding the American military presence on NATO's eastern flank.
items.body_text:
WASHINGTON -- US President Donald Trump says Washington and Warsaw are making "major progress" toward establishing a permanent US Army base in Poland, potentially expanding the American military presence on NATO's eastern flank.
"Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland," Trump said in a post on Truth Social on September 17. "If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance."
Nawrocki welcomed the announcement, saying Poland was ready to continue efforts to strengthen defense cooperation with Washington.
"I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base," Nawrocki said in a post on X.
The announcement came on the 87th anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland. Zbigniew Bogucki, head of the Polish president's chancellery, called the development "great news for Poland."
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said in August that Warsaw and Washington had already completed an initial stage of discussions on a possible permanent US military presence in Poland.
Polish and US officials held further talks in Warsaw on September 10 on strengthening the US military presence, with additional consultations and working groups planned.
The United States already has troops stationed in Poland, but they have largely been deployed on a rotational basis. Warsaw has reportedly been seeking a larger allied presence on NATO's eastern flank since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
US Force Posture Review
"The idea of a permanent US Army base in Poland is not entirely new," said Tom Nagy, senior research fellow for nuclear, space, and missile defense at GlobSec. It was already discussed during the first Trump administration, although it never ultimately materialized."
What's different this time, Nagy said, is "the broader context of the US force posture review, which has created expectations of potential troop reductions and even base closures in Western and Southern Europe."
The Pentagon's broader review has prompted concern among some lawmakers that diplomatic considerations could receive insufficient attention.
In a letter led by Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Senate Democrat on foreign policy, eight Democratic senators urged Secretary of State Marco Rubio to ensure that the State Department is fully involved in the review.
The lawmakers said decisions involving troop deployments, basing arrangements, status-of-forces agreements, and host-nation negotiations should be handled through an interagency process that takes both military and diplomatic considerations into account.
They also said US ambassadors and chiefs of mission in countries potentially affected by changes in troop deployments had not been adequately included in consultations.
The State Department has disputed the characterization that its officials have been excluded from the process.
A senior Western official familiar with the discussions told RFE/RL that the possible base in Poland is being considered as part of the broader US force-posture review. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the review could involve changes to the deployment of US forces elsewhere in Europe, including Germany.
Trump also spoke by phone with Chancellor Merz on September 17 about "next steps" toward ending the war in Ukraine, according to German government spokesman Stefan Kornelius.
Security Concerns
The discussions come as Poland faces heightened security concerns linked to Russia's war against Ukraine.
Polish authorities temporarily closed airports in Lublin and Rzeszow on September 17 as Russian strikes targeted parts of Ukraine, according to Polish officials.

items.title: White House Rejects UN Report Alleging US War Crimes In Iran
items.summary: As the conflict in the Persian Gulf continues to impact and shape the region, journalists from RFE/RL's Central Newsroom and Iranian service, Radio Farda, deliver ongoing updates and analysis.
items.body_text:
White House Rejects UN Report Alleging US War Crimes In Iran
The White House has rejected a report by a UN independent fact-finding mission that said there were reasonable grounds to believe the United States had committed war crimes during two air strikes in Iran.
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran said in a report released on September 17 that there were reasonable grounds to believe US forces committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks during strikes on a school in Minab and a sports facility in Lamerd on February 28.
The two strikes killed at least 178 civilians, including women and children, according to the mission. The Minab strike hit the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School and killed more than 150 people, including about 120 schoolchildren.
A separate strike on a sports complex and surrounding residential area in Lamerd killed 22 civilians.
In a scathing written response to the report, White House Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly rejected the findings, saying: "The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime, which has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region."
Kelly also said the UN Human Rights Council had "accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades."
US officials have repeatedly said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict and that an investigation is ongoing.
The report is scheduled to be formally presented to the 47-member UN Human Rights Council in Geneva on September 21.
The mission also found reasonable grounds to believe that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their crackdown on nationwide protests in December-January. It cited unlawful killings, arbitrary detention, torture, and other inhumane acts committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians.
IRGC Says It Struck Another Oil Tanker In Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Navy said on September 18 that it had struck another oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, setting the vessel on fire and forcing it to stop.
In a statement, the IRGC identified the tanker as the Trend, sailing under the Togolese flag. It said the vessel was struck on the night of September 17 while attempting what Iran described as an "illegal" passage through the vital waterway.
The IRGC said the tanker caught fire and was stopped. It did not provide information about the vessel's crew, cargo, possible casualties, or its current condition.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of the reported strike or fire.
Within the past 24 hours, the UK Maritime Trade Operations Organization (UKMTO) has issued three reports of security incidents involving vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, including one involving "a tanker being hit by an unknown projectile causing a fire onboard which has since been extinguished."
"All crew are reported safe and environmental impact is unconfirmed at present," the UKMTO added.
It remains unclear whether any of the UKMTO incidents involved the same vessel identified by the IRGC as the Trend.
The IRGC Navy said it maintains control of the Strait of Hormuz and warned that vessels attempting what it considers illegal passage would face destruction.
The United States has disputed Iran's claims of control over the waterway and has been assisting commercial vessels navigating the strait amid the conflict.
South Korea Rules Out Military Involvement in Iran War
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has ruled out sending troops or military assets to the Middle East in a way that would involve Seoul in the war with Iran, but said South Korea may take measures to protect commercial shipping and oil shipments through the region.

items.title: Russians Vote In First Parliamentary Election Since 2022 Ukraine Invasion
items.summary: Russians cast ballots to choose lawmakers for the State Duma, with the more-than-4 ½-year-old war on Ukraine and a slowing economy looming over the country’s first parliamentary elections since the 2022 invasion.
items.body_text:
Russians cast ballots to choose lawmakers for the State Duma, with the all-out war on Ukraine and a slowing economy looming over the country's first parliamentary elections since the start of the 2022 invasion.
Voters in the Pacific region of Kamchatka, nine time zones ahead of Moscow, kicked off the September 18-20 balloting. Official results on the new composition of the 450-seat lower house of parliament are expected by September 22.
United Russia, the Kremlin-linked party that dominates the Duma as well as legislatures and regional governments nationwide, is projected to maintain or increase its majority.
Since President Vladimir Putin came to power over a quarter-century ago, the Kremlin has increasingly stifled dissent, marginalized political opponents, and manipulated elections, leaving little room for surprises.
Meanwhile, the only prominent political party opposing the war, now in its fifth year, was barred from the ballot weeks ahead of the vote.
Amid Kremlin fears of apathy and frustration, Putin, who frequently accuses the West of seeking to weaken or destroy Russia, exhorted Russians to vote, calling the election a barometer of support for the war. More than 1.5 million Russian soldiers have been killed or wounded in the conflict, according to Western estimates.
"Your choice and your will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our troops, that we are a united people bound by shared values, historical memory, and love for the Motherland, and no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us or in undermining our sovereignty or our social-political system," Putin said in a speech released on September 16.
Russian authorities have set up voting precincts in the Russian-occupied portions of five Ukrainian regions that Moscow has claimed as Russian territory. Kyiv has denounced the effort.
While no dramatic changes are expected in the composition of the Duma, the Kremlin and the powerful domestic policymaking body known as the Presidential Administration were expected to watch results for hints of the national mood.
Though opinion polling is difficult inside Russia due to oppressive policies that have criminalized dissent or opposition to the war, several polls have pointed to slipping popularity for Putin, as well as United Russia.
Putin himself won reelection in 2024 in a vote that was seen largely as a foregone conclusion and was marred by evidence of fraud.
A growing number of Russians have grown impatient with the war, the largest in Europe since World War II. Russia's total casualties exceed those the country suffered in all wars Moscow has fought since 1945.
Ukraine's casualties are fewer overall but still staggeringly high.
Military commanders have consistently painted a rosy picture of how Russian troops are performing on the battlefield, and the Kremlin has repeatedly suggested that victory is assured.
Russians are also nervous about the potential for another mobilization, similar to the one Putin ordered in September 2022. That effort, which called up 300,000 men, mostly reservists, stunned Russian society, and led to an exodus of hundreds of thousands of people.
The economy, meanwhile, has downshifted sharply after months of torrid growth fueled by government spending on war-related things like soldiers' salaries, death benefits, and investment in armaments and weaponry.
The Central Bank has struggled to tame inflation running well above expectations.
A wide-ranging Ukrainian drone and missile campaign has caused fuel shortages across the country, and has disrupted the country's largest online retailers.
Russia's fractious and beleaguered opposition has called on people to vote for any candidates espousing an anti-war message.
However, the country's best-known liberal political party, Yabloko, was barred from fielding candidates in the Duma vote on a technicality. Yabloko had embraced an anti-war platform for the campaign, and some polls had indicated a sharp uptick in support.

items.title: Who gets to decide how quickly AI moves?
items.summary: The biggest AI companies want to slow development together. The real question is what power they gain in return.
items.body_text:
Who gets to decide how quickly AI moves?
The biggest AI companies want to slow development together. The real question is what power they gain in return.
Artificial intelligence (AI) has stirred up more controversy than most things in the past five years. Ever since the introduction of accessible generative AI in 2022, institutions, universities, students, scholars, activists, cognitive specialists, public policymakers and members of the public have all been divided over the ethics of its use. As of the beginning of this month, even the founders of AI companies have taken the same stance. Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, released an essay calling on AI companies to slow the development of their most advanced models, as the safeguards currently in place are unable to keep up. Shortly after Amodei’s essay, his position was endorsed by Sam Altman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind, and Satya Nadella of Microsoft. In addition, Sam Altman said that OpenAI will not be going public in 2026, as further safety advances are still required. While on the surface this may seem like a development in the collective conscience, the problem is far more multifaceted and layered – leaving the industry and the intended audience divided.
The products
Take a look at the products that each AI giant sells. Amodei, Altman, Musk and Hassabis sell models, while Nadella sells the cloud those models run on. Both groups have advised slowing down. On the other hand, Jensen Huang, founder, president, and CEO of Nvidia, sells the chips that these companies buy before they can build anything. Huang does not advise a slowdown and has instead asserted that AI does not need new legislation because market forces can push companies towards safe innovation without the need for regulation. Mark Zuckerberg, whose company gives its models for free, warned that the proposal could expose companies to greater legal risks.
The common thread between these divisive recommendations is profit. Some companies will benefit from a slowdown, while others will earn greater profits by moving faster. Nvidia’s ability to charge high prices has benefitted from the intense competition between these AI companies, which fear falling behind their rivals. If this competitive pressure decreases, companies may be less willing to pay a premium for Nvidia’s chips. Hence, Huang’s opposition to the proposal may reflect both genuine concerns and Nvidia’s commercial interests.
The word the White House used
In the world of AI, antitrust law prevents these companies from holding private meetings to decide what they can and cannot do. This is intended to prevent them from coordinating the pace of development and engaging in unfair competition. However, some of these AI companies have now come forward arguing that they should be allowed to work outside antitrust law for the sake of technological safety. Huang and David Sacks, the White House AI lead, have been critical of this request, as it could reduce competition and increase the influence of these AI companies over their rivals. Sacks also questioned the independence of nonprofit evaluators tasked with evaluating AI safety “independently”. In essence, he asks: how is it fair for one company to inspect another?
The clause that travels badly
Amodei’s proposal would deny China access to the most powerful AI chips and advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and prevent smuggling and remote access to computing capacity abroad. China’s foreign ministry countered the proposal, saying that these warnings are a fearmongering tactic aimed at slowing down China’s technological advancement, echoing the Cold War. Amodei did admit that China poses the toughest predicament for his plan. Despite its alleged advantages, the proposal gives American firms leverage over Chinese ones.

Asian Games organisers in Japan accidently play North Korea’s anthem ahead of South’s during hockey match with Bangladesh.
The South Korean men’s hockey team were left bemused before their Asian Games match against Bangladesh on Friday when North Korea’s national anthem was played instead of their own.
Lined up before the match, the South Korean players looked around in confusion as the anthem rang out at Green Stadium in Gifu, Japan.

items.body_text:
سفينة حربية إيطالية "متقاعدة" تصبح أول حاملة طائرات لإندونيسيا
استقبلت إندونيسيا اليوم الجمعة أول حاملة طائرات في تاريخها، هي سفينة حربية إيطالية سابقة عمرها 41 عاما، في أحدث صفقة كبيرة لشراء أسلحة، في وقت تسعى فيه جاكرتا إلى تحديث معداتها العسكرية المتقادمة.
وبعد إبحارها من إيطاليا مرورا بكولومبو ومضيق ملقا رست السفينة الإيطالية السابقة "إتس جوزيبي جاريبالدي"، صباح اليوم إلى قاعدة بحرية في ميناء تانجونج بريوك بشمال جاكرتا، حيث تم استقبالها بمراسم عسكرية.
القدرات
ويعود تاريخ تدشين السفينة في إيطاليا إلى41 عاما مضت، وتتمتع بقدرة على استيعاب طائرات الإقلاع القصير والهبوط العمودي والمروحيات.
قصص مقترحة
list of 2 items
ويمكن للسفينة البالغ طولها 180 مترا، حمل ما يصل إلى 18 مروحية واستيعاب طاقم يصل إلى 830 فردا، حسبما أوضح المتحدث باسم البحرية الإندونيسية تونغول.
ومن المقرر أن تدخل الحاملة رسميا الخدمة في القوات البحرية الإندونيسية الأسبوع المقبل باسم "كي آر آي سريويجايا"، نسبة إلى القائد العسكري الشهير في إمبراطورية ماجاباهيت في القرن الـ14، والذي جعلت منه حملاته ورؤيته لأرخبيل موحد واحدا من أكثر الشخصيات التاريخية احتفاء بها في إندونيسيا.
هاجس الكوارث
وصرح رئيس أركان البحرية الإندونيسية محمد علي أن تركز مهامها على العمليات غير العسكرية، بما في ذلك عمليات الإغاثة في حالات الكوارث.
وقال علي "تشهد البلاد كوارث عديدة، لذا نحن بحاجة ماسة إلى سفينة أو منصة قادرة على حمل أعداد كبيرة من المروحيات، لأن المروحيات قادرة على إنزال الإمدادات اللوجيستية بسرعة في المناطق النائية".
وتابع "حالة السفينة لا تزال جيدة جدا، ونأمل أن تتمكن البحرية الإندونيسية من استخدامها للسنوات الـ15 أو الـ20 المقبلة".
ومن شأن هذا الانتقال أن يجعل إندونيسيا ثاني دولة فقط في جنوب شرق آسيا تمتلك حاملة طائرات في أسطولها.
وكانت الدولة الأولى هي تايلند التي تمتلك السفينة "إتش تي إم إس شاكري ناريبت"، والتي دخلت الخدمة في عام 1997 بعد شرائها من إسبانيا إلى جانب طائرات "إيه في-8 إس ماتادور" القادرة على العمل من على متن الحاملات.
وكانت إيطاليا قد وافقت في مارس/أذار الماضي على إهداء حاملة الطائرات، التي أحيلت إلى التقاعد في عام 2024، إلى إندونيسيا في خطوة تهدف إلى تعزيز المشاركة الدفاعية الأوسع لإيطاليا مع الدولة الواقعة في جنوب شرق آسيا.
وتسعى إيطاليا إلى إبرام صفقات غواصات وطائرات، كما أن إهداء الحاملة لإندونيسيا يوفر عليها أيضا تكلفة تفكيك السفينة وإخراجها من الخدمة.
تشكيك
وشكك محللون في جدوى الاستحواذ على هذه الحاملة، مشيرين إلى أنها ستحتاج على الأرجح إلى أعمال صيانة، ولفتوا إلى أن إندونيسيا تواجه تحديات أكثر إلحاحا، مثل الديون الخارجية.
ورأى محمد فوزان مالوفتي، الباحث في مركز الدراسات الإستراتيجية والدولية، أن السفينة قد لا تكون فعالة في حالات النزاع العسكري.
وقال "إذا كانت وظيفتها الأساسية هي الإغاثة في حالات الكوارث، فقد تكون تسليحاتها محدودة جدا"، مضيفا أن ذلك قد يقلص أكثر من القدرات القتالية للحاملة. مؤكدا أن الحكومة الإندونيسية أجرت "تقييما شاملا قبل المضي في عملية الشراء".
تحديث
ويسعى الرئيس الإندونيسي برابوو سوبيانتو، وهو جنرال سابق انتُخب عام 2024، إلى تحديث العتاد العسكري الإندونيسي المتقادم وتعزيز التعاون الدفاعي مع دول أخرى.
ووقّعت جاكرتا صفقة بقيمة 8.1 مليارات دولار في عام 2022، يوم كان برابوو يشغل منصب وزير الدفاع، لشراء 42 طائرة مقاتلة فرنسية الصنع طراز رافال، تم تسليم 6 طائرات منها في مايو/أيار الماضي.
وطلبت إندونيسيا شراء غواصتين طراز "سكوربين" من شركة الدفاع الفرنسية نافال غروب في عام 2024، وقد بدأت عملية بنائهما في أغسطس/آب، وفق بيان للشرك.
كما أكدت الهند في يوليو/تموز الماضي، تزامنا مع استقبال الرئيس برابوو لرئيس الوزراء الهندي ناريندرا مودي في جاكرتا، أنها ستزود إندونيسيا بصواريخ بعيدة المدى.
وفي فبراير/شباط الماضي، وقّعت إندونيسيا اتفاقية أمنية مع أستراليا، مهدت لتعاون عسكري أوثق يتضمن دعم كانبيرا لتطوير مرافق تدريب مخصصة للمناورات المشتركة.

items.title: بطولة كأس الخليج.. ملتقى "لمّ الشمل" عبر التاريخ
items.summary: لطالما كانت بطولة كأس الخليج ملتقى للمّ الشمل بين الدول الخليجية، وقد شهدت مسيرتها منذ البداية العديد من التطورات والمراحل.
items.body_text:
بطولة كأس الخليج.. ملتقى "لمّ الشمل" عبر التاريخ
رغبة في التقارب بين منتخبات المنطقة وتجميعها في بطولة دورية، أبصرت كأس الخليج لكرة القدم النور عام 1970 في البحرين، فحظيت باهتمام لافت وارتفعت فيها وتيرة التنافس بين الجيران بصرف النظر عن فارق المستوى والجاهزية الفنية.
خلال عشاء عام 1968 في الرياض، طرح الأمير خالد الفيصل، مدير عام رعاية الشباب السعودية، على الشيخ محمد بن خليفة آل خليفة، رئيس الاتحاد البحريني المهتم باستضافة مباريات ودية للأندية والمنتخبات، فكرة عفوية بلمّ شمل منتخبات المنطقة في بطولة واحدة.
قصص مقترحة
list of 2 items
نالت ترحيبا من المسؤولين السياسيين، فاحتضنت البحرين النسخة الأولى في عام 1970، بعدما عُرضت الفكرة على رئيس الاتحاد الدولي (فيفا) الإنجليزي ستانلي راوس في أولمبياد مكسيكو عام 1968.
اشتهرت بطولة الخليج في بداياتها، بوجود الثلاثي الإداري الشهير الأمير فيصل بن فهد رئيس الاتحاد السعودي والشيخ فهد الأحمد رئيس الاتحاد الكويتي والشيخ عيسى بن راشد رئيس الاتحاد البحريني، حيث ساهموا في نهضتها من خلال تصريحاتهم القوية، فيما نُقل عن الشيخ فهد الأحمد قوله بعد غياب المنتخب السعودي عن إحراز اللقب، إنه لن يحققها إلا إذا أصبحت الكرة مربعة!
شاركت أربع دول في النسخة الافتتاحية، هي البحرين والسعودية والكويت وقطر، فيما توّجت الكويت بلقب أول نسخة بثلاثة انتصارات عن جدارة بعد ظهورها بمستوى عال، ممهدة الطريق لسجل قياسي يتضمن عشرة ألقاب من أصل 26 نسخة.
على هامش الدورة الأولى، تقرّر إقامتها كل سنتين بدلا من تنظيمها سنويا، واحتفاظ المتوج ثلاث مرات بالكأس إلى الأبد، كما هي الحال في كأس جول ريميه القديمة لكأس العالم.
في أيار/مايو 1977، عُقد اجتماع لممثلي الاتحادات الخليجية في الإمارات، فطُرح اقتراحان ينصّ الأول على إقامة الدورة كل ثلاث سنوات والثاني يتبنى إقامتها كل سنتين.
ونظرا لعدم اكتمال المنشآت الرياضية في الإمارات، اعتذرت عن عدم احتضان الدورة الخامسة، فاستضافها العراق في عام 1979.
أحرز العراق مع هدافه حسين سعيد اللقب عن جدارة أمام الكويت التي منيت بخسارتها الأولى، فيما برز السعودي ماجد عبدالله.
افتتاح قطري وتوهج سعودي
تبادل العراق والكويت الألقاب حتى النسخة الحادية عشرة في قطر عام 1992 على استاد خليفة الدولي، حيث توّج العنابي مرة أولى، في ظل غياب العراق الممنوع من المشاركة بسبب حرب الخليج الثانية.
دخلت السعودية على خط الألقاب فتوّجت ثلاث مرات بين عامي 1994 و2004، فيما راح لقبان للبطل الاعتيادي الكويت في عامي 1996 و1998 بفعل تألق جاسم الهويدي وبدر حجي.
في عام 2003، شارك اليمن للمرة الأولى، بقرار من قادة دول مجلس التعاون الخليجي، لكن نصيبه كان المركز الأخير بنقطة واحدة من ست مباريات.
اللقب الثاني لقطر أحرزته أيضا على أرضها في عام 2004، عندما عاد العراق للمشاركة، فيما انتظرت الإمارات حتى عام 2007 لتظفر بلقبها الأول في أبوظبي بهدف نجمها إسماعيل مطر في النهائي ضد عُمان.
وللمرة الثالثة تواليا توّجت الدولة المضيفة، عندما أحرزت عُمان اللقب الأول في عام 2009 على حساب السعودية، معوضة خيبة الخسارة مرتين في النهائي.
اتجهت البطولة إلى اليمن للمرة الأولى نهاية عام 2010، رغم شكوك حول إقامتها بسبب الأوضاع الأمنية، وهناك عزّزت الكويت مع فهد العنزي وبدر المطوّع رقمها القياسي محرزة لقبها العاشر.
الأبطال الجدد.. ولقب ثالث للعنابي
أظهر منتخب الإمارات بقيادة المدرب مهدي علي تطوّره، فزحفت جماهيره جوا وبحرا لدعم زملاء عمر عبد الرحمن في رحلة التتويج بلقب عام 2013 في البحرين.
رفعت قطر ألقابها إلى ثلاثة على حساب المضيفة السعودية نهاية عام 2014 بحضور جماهيري كبير في الرياض، فتوجت للمرة الأولى خارج أرضها.
وأحرزت عُمان لقبها الثاني مطلع عام 2018 في الكويت، وبركلات الترجيح أيضا، عندما تألق حارسها فايز الرشيدي في النهائي ضد الإمارات، ثم تُوّج المنتخب البحريني بلقبه الأول نهاية عام 2019 على حساب السعودية بهدف.
على أرضه، توج العراق مطلع عام 2023 بلقبه الرابع والأول منذ عام 1988 بفوز دراماتيكي قاتل على عمان 3-2 في البصرة، بهدف مناف يونس في الدقيقة 120+2 أمام أكثر من 65 ألف متفرج.
وفي النسخة الأخيرة في الكويت مطلع عام 2025، حصدت البحرين لقبها الثاني في غضون خمس سنوات، عندما قلبت تأخرها أمام عمان إلى فوز 2-1 في الدقائق الأخيرة.
