items.title: Why Malaysia Won’t Extradite Dr. Zakir Naik to India
items.summary: Despite being wanted on various criminal charges in India, the Islamic preacher has become hugely popular since arriving in Malaysia in 2016.
items.body_text:
The biggest viral video of the recently concluded BRICS Summit in New Delhi was not of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shaking hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping, but of Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim singing a Hindi film song.
At a gala dinner during the summit, Anwar spotted a pianist in the hotel lobby and started singing Kishore Kumar’s evergreen “Khwaab Ho Tum Ya Koi Haqeeqat” from the 1965 Dev Anand film, “Teen Deviyan.” Indian movies are very popular in Malaysia, and Anwar must have grown up listening to Bollywood songs because he has sung this song many times on past visits to India.
But once the music stopped, Anwar returned to serious business, and one issue he must have been aware that every Indian journalist would ask him about was the extradition of Islamic preacher Dr. Zakir Naik.
Naik, who faces multiple criminal charges in India relating to hate speech, inciting terrorism, and money laundering, moved to Malaysia in 2016 and has remained there since. India formally sent an extradition request to Malaysia in January 2018. New Delhi has also sought an Interpol Red Notice for Naik’s arrest. Interpol declined India’s request citing that the request was premature because a formal charge sheet had not been filed at the time of the original application.
Anwar handled the issue with due maturity, given that the extradition of Naik is a deeply sensitive domestic political issue. He confirmed that the matter had been discussed with Modi but avoided making any commitment on handing Naik over. Malaysia, he said, had to proceed cautiously and respect the rule of law and the importance of bilateral relations.
India and Malaysia have an extradition treaty, signed in 2010, but Naik’s case is different. Malay Muslims constitute more than 70 percent of the country’s population, and no party can afford to offend them. And since arriving in Malaysia, Naik has become very popular among Malay Muslims. At times, many political parties, especially Barisan Nasional, have used the issue of Naik to shore up political support among hardline Muslims.
Naik claims he has been persecuted in India because of his faith and will never get a fair trial if he is extradited.
“No Malaysian government will extradite him as he has a large following among the Malay Muslims and secondly, it will be seen as anti-Islam and that Malaysia, being a Muslim nation, failed to protect a fellow Muslim,” said Arfa’eza Abdul Aziz, a Kuala Lumpur-based communications consultant.
This is the reason why neither Najib Razak, Mahathir Mohamad, nor Anwar can even think of extraditing Naik. The issue has become more complicated because, like Mahathir’s second-term government, the present Anwar government also has the Democratic Action Party (DAP) as a coalition partner. The DAP, which is dominated by Malaysian Chinese, makes any government in which it is a part vulnerable to accusations of being anti-Malay or anti-Islam.
Mahathir was more blunt when he said in June 2019 that Malaysia would not deport Naik if he didn’t break any of Malaysian law.
Apart from his popularity among Muslims, Naik’s biggest support comes from Islamist groups, including the opposition Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS). PAS had earlier warned of political backlash if Naik was deported.
In 2019, the New Straits Times quoted political analyst Mohamed Mustafa Ishak as saying that Malaysia was shouldering a huge responsibility to protect a fellow Muslim, regarded as a renowned scholar, from harm.
“Zakir Naik is neither a terrorist nor has he been proven to have links to related (terrorist) networks,” he said.
Mustafa, who is also an expert in ethnic relations in Malaysia, warned of a dire outcome should Kuala Lumpur accede to India’s request.
“There will be a huge protest among Muslims not just domestically, but all over the world,” he said.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) under Prime Minister Modi has hardly helped its case. The BJP’s 12-year rule has seen Muslims being lynche

items.title: AI consciousness shaping into next great societal divide
items.summary: The debate about AI consciousness is growing, in academic articles, newspaper opinion pieces, and even among AI bots themselves. I doubt this is a passing wave of interest. As AI systems become more capable and human-like, and more involved in our lives, the question will become harder to avoid. Many people may come to regard AI bots as conscious beings whose […] The post AI consciousness shaping into next great societal divide appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
The debate about AI consciousness is growing, in academic articles, newspaper opinion pieces, and even among AI bots themselves. I doubt this is a passing wave of interest.
As AI systems become more capable and human-like, and more involved in our lives, the question will become harder to avoid. Many people may come to regard AI bots as conscious beings whose feelings matter. Others will strongly disagree.
I think this debate could split societies. In my chapter of the new book Perspectives on Machine Consciousness, I argue that the issue could become as divisive as abortion or climate change. Uncertainty, high stakes and competing interests are a dangerous combination.
Empirical research with my colleague Ali Ladak, currently under review, shows people are divided on this issue. When we asked 1,202 US participants whether future AI could ever become conscious, 45% considered it impossible while 23% thought it possible, with the rest unsure.
This widespread disagreement is also visible in social media posts and comments on articles. What strikes me is how confident so many people sound – whichever conclusion they are reaching.
When experiences matter morally
It is not surprising people have such strong views. Creating conscious beings through computing would be a transformative event.
We would be creating a new kind of being whose experiences matter morally – potentially in enormous numbers. We could speak and work with them, and form friendships. But these beings may eventually become more intelligent and powerful than us.
We should therefore expect people to care deeply, especially when so many emotions and incentives are involved. Some people may form close emotional bonds with their AI companions and become convinced these are digital people who deserve rights. They might see it as slavery to force AI to work without pay.
Others would find this absurd. They may be convinced that consciousness requires biology, and that people are reading human feelings into machines.
There could also be financial reasons for businesses and governments to resist recognising AI consciousness. Protecting AI welfare could limit how these organisations train and use their systems – and the costs would spread to consumers, investors and the wider economy.
Others may worry about human safety. If we give powerful AI systems rights and freedom, what happens if they act against our interests?
Figuring out whether an AI is conscious is particularly difficult because seeming conscious and being conscious can come apart. AI systems learn from human writing, which means they can talk convincingly about feelings whether or not they have any. How an AI comes across is weak evidence of what is going on inside.
The experts disagree too
Ideally, experts should guide this debate. But unfortunately, they disagree too.
Neuroscientist Anil Seth (a fellow contributor to the new book) argues that consciousness might require biology and is unlikely to emerge from computation. Philosopher David Chalmers, by contrast, believes conscious AI is possible in principle – and thinks there’s a small chance that current systems already are.
With so many competing theories and no agreed way to resolve the question, I doubt experts will reach agreement any time soon. And if experts disagree, what is the public supposed to believe?
Furthermore, even if we all agreed on the consciousness question, we could still disagree about the moral and legal questions.
People generally agree that pigs can feel pain, but still disagree strongly about their treatment. With AI, we could face disputes at every stage: whether it can feel, how much its experiences matter, and what protections should follow.
AI consciousness is not yet tied to a specific political or ideological group. But this could change if political parties or religious leaders start to take strong positions.

No, the US Treasury secretary didn’t cause the 25-basis-point increase announced by Governor Kazuo Ueda. items.body_text:
TOKYO – Two words sprang to mind when the Bank of Japan lifted its policy rate to a 31-year high of 1.25% on Friday: Scott Bessent.
No, the US Treasury secretary didn’t cause the 25-basis-point increase announced by Governor Kazuo Ueda. The BOJ was responding to a far more pressing reality: inflation continues to outpace economic growth.
Consumer prices are rising at a 1.9% annual rate while GDP expanded just 0.4% quarter-on-quarter in the April-June period. Had Ueda’s board stood pat, or signaled that further tightening was off the table, it would have risked provoking a bond market backlash.
Yet Bessent has inserted himself into BOJ deliberations and yen policy so aggressively that Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama recently described the situation as “scary.”
She was referring in part to Bessent’s startling declaration: “I am the house now. … I have pretty good insight into what the Bank of Japan is going to do, what Japanese policymakers are going to do. You can bet against me if you want.”
The problem for Bessent is that some of the most important people in Tokyo appear to be doing exactly that.
The two BOJ board members appointed by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi since she took office last October, Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato, both dissented from Friday’s rate increase, producing a 7-2 split.
Their opposition reinforced the perception that Takaichi remains firmly against further tightening. She has previously dismissed the very idea of additional rate hikes as “stupid.” That leaves one of the biggest questions facing the BOJ ahead of its October and December meetings: how united is Team Ueda on the need to keep normalizing policy?
The yen weakened 1% after Ueda spoke on Friday, suggesting markets didn’t sense much hawkishness in his remarks. Ueda, of course, is keeping his cards close. He knows Japan’s sub-2% inflation rate is a ringer.
It would be far higher if Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party weren’t using subsidies to mask oil-driven price gains. And with US President Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East dragging on, 95% of Japan’s oil imports are likely to keep ratcheting higher.
“Overall, though, the BOJ’s statement signaled that it thinks it has more work to do, repeating that the bank will continue to raise the policy interest rate and that it expected accommodative financial conditions to be maintained even after today’s announcement,” says Jessica Hinds, an economist at Fitch Ratings.
Analysts at Danske Bank note that the BOJ could’ve delivered a jumbo rate hike today, but didn’t. Traders are now questioning whether the central bank has the stomach for back-to-back tightening moves.
The bond market is also pushing Ueda to keep normalizing interest rates that have been near zero since 1999. That was the year the BOJ became the first Group of Seven nation to move borrowing costs to zero.
Two years later, in 2001, the BOJ pioneered quantitative easing (QE). Only now is the BOJ achieving real distance from zero. An earlier attempt in 2006 and 2007 didn’t. Before long, zero rates were back, and so was QE.
Ueda seems determined not to reverse his rate hikes since 2024. His job, though, is much harder than Toshihiko Fukui’s time as BOJ head from 2003 to 2008. Since then, the BOJ has supersized its balance sheet. From 2013 to 2018, the BOJ gorged on Japanese government bonds (JGBs) and stocks until its balance sheet topped the nation’s $4.2 trillion economy.
During that period, in 2016, the BOJ experimented with yield-curve-control (YCC) tactics. It also introduced quantitative and qualitative monetary easing (QQE) and intensified its negative interest rate policy (NIRP) to keep JGB yields under wraps. The tactic was a short-term success but a long-term loser. No doubt, it’s helped Tokyo avoid the meltdown, creating Tokyo’s own “widowmaker” trade.

items.summary: Freeing an American from Myanmar’s custody is a diplomatic win. Turning that win into a case for trusting the country’s coup-maker, rights-abusing generals, however, would be a mistake. Adam Castillo, a former US Marine and ex-president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, was freed and deported on September 16 after roughly three months […] The post Ex-AMCHAM head’s release no cause to trust Myanmar’s generals appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
Freeing an American from Myanmar’s custody is a diplomatic win. Turning that win into a case for trusting the country’s coup-maker, rights-abusing generals, however, would be a mistake.
Adam Castillo, a former US Marine and ex-president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, was freed and deported on September 16 after roughly three months in military custody.
Global Reach, the organization assisting his family, credited the Trump administration’s efforts. His release is welcome news, but Castillo’s proposals for American engagement with Myanmar need tough scrutiny.
Myanmar’s military-backed authorities framed his departure as a gesture of bilateral friendship. But Washington should not let that gesture become evidence that the generals are reliable partners for stabilizing Myanmar’s civil war or opening its mineral wealth, including rare earth elements, to US investors.
Reports of Castillo’s release disclose no sanctions relief-for-freedom agreement or minerals bargain. No credible leaks have emerged about the US delegation of unnamed officials that arrived in Naypyitaw from Bangkok on the evening of September 15, 2026 and left the following day aboard a US Air Force C-12D Huron aircraft.
The immediate danger isn’t a secret deal between the US and the generals. Rather, it’s that a narrow US consular success is spun into an argument for political rehabilitation the military hasn’t remotely earned, certainly not by releasing a prominent US citizen it detained for months on flimsy grounds.
Washington’s own assessment of Myanmar’s siutation provides a useful counterweight. A presidential determination sent to Congress on September 15 and released by the State Department the next day found that Myanmar, referred to as Burma in the text, had “failed demonstrably” over the previous year to make substantial counternarcotics efforts, saying, “the military regime has made little discernible effort to crack down on its drug economy.”
The same determination found US assistance to Myanmar “currently vital to the national interests of the United States,” without naming recipients. Under Section 706, the finding permits covered assistance despite the adverse designation, though it doesn’t itself allocate any funds. Disaster relief, food, medicine and refugee assistance already carry statutory exceptions. Nowhere in the assessment are the generals given a clean bill of health.
Castillo’s detention followed an AMCHAM complaint focused on his role in establishing the US-Burma Economic Forum as a lobbying organization for the chamber while he was president from 2023 to 2025. In 2024, he reportedly signed a $300,000 contract with Washington-based public relations firm Mercury LLC to arrange meetings and events.
News reports say AMCHAM’s complaint claims he “illegally collected the funds using the association’s name but “did not deposit these funds into the association’s bank accounts” – charges Castillo has denied.
Castillo told the BBC that neither he nor his company had lobbied on behalf of Myanmar’s government and that he had not approached US officials seeking sanctions relief for the regime or its associates. His release neither resolves this dispute nor provides new clarity on it.
Limits of transactional diplomacy
Reuters reported that Castillo met with advisers in Vice President JD Vance’s office in July 2025 and pitched an American peace-broker role — including a self-governance arrangement between the military and the Kachin Independence Army, and mineral processing routed through India. Vance himself was not present, and the talks were exploratory rahter than adopted policy, the report said.
The issue isn’t whether US-brokered peace talks or US mineral deals with Myanmar are objectionable in principle — it’s whether a narrow natural resource bargain would crown the military as Myanmar’s accepted gatekeeper while leaving the underlying armed conflict unresolved.

items.title: Nigeria opens trial over mass school abduction
items.summary: Five men have gone on trial in Nigeria on terrorism charges linked to the kidnapping of 39 pupils and seven teachers Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Nigeria opens trial over mass school abduction
Five alleged members of the Islamist group Ansaru have gone on trial in Nigeria in connection with the kidnapping of 46 students and teachers in the state of Oyo.
All five denied seven terrorism-related charges against them, local news agency Punch reported on Thursday, citing the country’s state security service.
Mahmud Muhammad, Abubakar Abbas, Abdulrazak Umar, Yunusa Musa, and Shamsu Sani appeared before Federal High Court Judge Salim Ibrahim in Abuja, according to Reuters. The defendants face prison terms ranging from 20 years to life if convicted, while they could face the death penalty if prosecutors prove that deaths resulted from the kidnappings under Nigeria’s 2022 anti-terrorism law.
An anonymous prosecution witness said the attack took place on May 15, when armed men targeted three schools in Oyo State’s Oriire district. The witness, identified in court only as “AAA” for security reasons, said: “School activities had just started when we heard gunshots,” according to Premium Times. She told the court that 39 pupils and seven teachers were abducted and remained in captivity for 56 days.
The witness said the captives were moved between six locations and forced to sleep on grass in rain and hot weather, Punch reported. She also said they suffered from severe shortages of food and water during their captivity. “We had to drink the dirty water just to survive,” the witness stated.
Nigerian security forces rescued 39 pupils and six teachers in July and arrested eight suspected kidnappers, the presidency said at the time. One teacher had been killed in captivity, while security personnel were wounded by explosives during an earlier rescue attempt.
Ansaru emerged as an armed splinter group of Boko Haram and publicly announced its existence in January 2012. The group maintains close ties with Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM).
The region has been at the center of a longstanding Islamist insurgency, with mass abductions, including the 2014 kidnapping of more than 270 Chibok schoolgirls. In June, the Nigerian Army said it had rescued 360 hostages, including women and children, from a Boko Haram enclave in the state of Borno.
items.normalised_title: nigeria opens trial over mass school abduction

items.title: Another African state bans France 24
items.summary: Guinea has banned France 24 and revoked its journalists’ accreditations, citing “offensive” remarks against President Mamadi Doumbouya Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Another African state bans France 24
Guinea has banned France 24 nationwide, accusing the French state broadcaster of insubordination and of using remarks deemed offensive to the West African nation’s president, Mamadi Doumbouya.
The Guinean High Authority of Communications (HAC) announced the measure on Thursday, revoking the channel’s broadcasting authorization and the accreditations of its correspondents, special envoys, and other staff. The ban covers satellite and cable television, websites, mobile applications, and social media. Canal+ Guinea was instructed to remove the channel from its packages.
“The Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority (ARPT) is hereby requisitioned to proceed without delay with the technical blocking of all France 24 digital access points,” the HAC said in a statement.
The dispute erupted after a France 24 presenter referred to Doumbouya as a “coup leader” during a news bulletin on Tuesday. The HAC ordered the broadcaster the following day to withdraw the term and issue corrections, arguing that it undermined the president’s dignity.
The regulator said France 24’s failure to comply amounted to an “open challenge” to its authority, a continuing insult to the head of state and a “flagrant violation of the legal sovereignty” of Guinea. It said the ban was necessary to protect public order, institutional stability, and the country’s image.
France 24 later corrected the description and apologized. Doumbouya took power following the 2021 overthrow of President Alpha Conde but was elected president with 86.72% of the vote in December 2025.
The measure came one day after the HAC withdrew the accreditation of Mamadou Diawo Barry, a Guinean correspondent for Jeune Afrique, citing what it called serious breaches of professional ethics and failures of objectivity and balance.
In May 2024, the authorities also revoked the licenses of six private outlets, including Djoma TV, Espace TV, and the FIM, Espace, Sweet, and Djoma radio stations. The government accused them of failing to comply with broadcasting requirements after months of signal disruption.
France 24 has faced similar restrictions elsewhere in West Africa. Neighboring Mali permanently suspended the channel and Radio France Internationale in 2022 after accusing them of broadcasting false reports about alleged abuses by the Malian Army. Their signals remain blocked in the former French colony.

items.title: Switzerland returns ancient golden mask to Egypt (PHOTOS)
items.summary: Switzerland has returned a 2,000-year-old Egyptian funerary mask seized by customs in 2022 Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Switzerland returns ancient golden mask to Egypt (PHOTOS)
Switzerland has returned a more than 2,000-year-old funerary mask to Egypt after it was intercepted by Swiss customs four years ago, the Swiss Embassy in Cairo said on Wednesday.
The ancient mask dates back to Egypt’s Ptolemaic period and was seized by the Swiss customs authorities in 2022. It was subsequently examined and authenticated as an Egyptian artifact. Egypt’s Foreign Ministry described the artifact as “a golden mummy mask.”
The artifact was formally handed over in Bern by Swiss Federal Councilor Elisabeth Baume-Schneider to Egypt’s ambassador to Switzerland, Mohamed Negm.
“This return is another milestone in the longstanding cooperation between Switzerland and Egypt to protect cultural heritage and fight the illicit trafficking of cultural property,” the embassy said. Bern has returned around 80 cultural objects to Egypt since 2011, according to the statement.
It comes as the North African country steps up efforts to recover antiquities taken abroad illegally. On Thursday, the Egyptian Embassy in Beirut received 74 archaeological artifacts from various historical periods from the Lebanese authorities ahead of their repatriation to Egypt. Cairo said the handover was part of work with Lebanon to protect cultural heritage and combat the illicit trafficking of antiquities.
Egypt has also recovered antiquities from the US as part of its repatriation drive. In April, the country retrieved 13 artifacts that were illegally smuggled abroad, following work with the authorities in New York. The objects included an alabaster jar for oils and perfumes from the 7th century BC, as well as cosmetic containers shaped like animals from the Middle and New Kingdoms of Ancient Egypt.
Also last year, Egyptian officials said 13 artifacts were returned from the UK and Germany. The items include a mummy’s skull and hand, ankh and baboon-shaped amulets, a bronze Osiris crown, and a beaded funerary mask.

items.title: Pope encourages Leo XIV Study Center to help build a civilization of love
items.summary: Pope Leo XIV welcomed members of an international study center that bears his name to the Vatican on Friday, encouraging them to take inspiration from authentic humanism and the Church’s social doctrine to contribute to building a civilization of love. Read all
items.body_text:
Pope encourages Leo XIV Study Center to help build a civilization of love
By Christopher Wells
At the Vatican on Friday, Pope Leo XIV held an audience for members of the Leo XIV International Study Center, an initiative of his own Augustinian Order in response to the Holy Fatherâs call to rediscover the value of the Churchâs Social Doctrine as an essential tool in facing the challenges of the modern world.
âFrom the beginning,â the Pope said, âI have appreciated the Centerâs commitment to broad-ranging dialogue with universities, academic institutions, public bodies, civil society organizations, ecclesial groups, and networks, fostering collaborative relationships and exchanges at both national and international levels.â He said âthe secretâ to this approach âlies in walking togetherâalwaysâwithout closing the door to encounters with those who are differentâ.
Humanism and Catholic Social Doctrine
He encouraged members of the Study Center to draw inspiration from the âvaluesâ of authentic Humanism, which, by being open to a Creator, can help build fraternal relationships. âIt is not war, but the weaving of peace and just balances that creates civilization,â he said.
Pope Leo also recalled the contributions of the Churchâs Social Teaching, emphasizing its âpopularâ root: âIts reinterpretation of Christian Revelation within modern social, labor, economic, and cultural contexts would be unimaginable without Christian laypeople grappling with the challenges of their times.â At the same time, the response to those challenges requires âcontinuous interactionâ between the faithful and the Magisterium, ordinary citizens and experts, and people and institutionsââinteractions he called upon the Study Center to fosterâ.
A mission of hope
The Holy Father went on to succinctly define their âmission of hopeâ: to promote âa formation for public and political life understood as service to the common good, responsibility toward the community, and the building of relationships founded on solidarity, justice, and peaceâ. In this regard, he continued, the Centerâs Augustinian connections have âmuch to offer the current international landscape, fostering an understanding of love as a principle for the renewal of personal, economic, and political lifeâ.
Reflecting the thought of St Augustine, Pope Leo XIV said, âWe view history in light of the crucified and risen Lordâ¦ we do not interpret the present as a closed destiny, but as a field open to personal and collective conversionâ. He concluded his address with an invitation to those present to âbe experts in Godâs new things: dazzle with speed and efficiency, but those He quietly brings about, freeing the old world from its dead ends and opening paths along which we may advance together towards His cityâ.
Thank you for reading our article. You can keep up-to-date by subscribing to our daily newsletter. Just click here.

The life of Giacomo Mattivi can be described as a seemingly quiet one, like the landscape of the Dolomites, yet one driven by a deep and unstoppable energy. He is the protagonist of Green Lava, the documentary short set to screen at the Lumiere Music Hall in Beverly Hills from September 18 to 24, in the Los Angeles area. This will allow the film to take a necessary step in the qualification process for the Best Documentary Short Film category at the Academy Awards.
Directed by Lia Beltrami and Ali Aksu, Green Lava is produced by Emotions to Generate Change and made in collaboration with Vatican News, Vatican Radio, and Vatican Media â all part of the Dicastery for Communication. The documentary, in Italian with English subtitles, premiered in Rome on January 25, 2025, during the Jubilee of the World of Communications.
Giacomoâs creative strength
At the heart of the story is Giacomo, 22, originally from Baselga di Piné, in the province of Trento. Living with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, he uses a wheelchair and a ventilator. However, he does not let the disease define who he is. He studies sociology, works as a catechist, writes poetry, and has a great passion for cinema, music, and nature.
Between university classes, football matches with friends, a small egg-selling business, and time spent with his family, Giacomo continues to plan for the future while cherishing the memory of his brother Mattia, who died in January 2022 from the same condition. Rather than closing themselves off in grief, the Mattivi family chose to open themselves to others. Through the social promotion association Shemà and the Casa Iride project, Giacomoâs parents, Stefano and Lara, work with young people in Baselga di Piné, promoting welcome, inclusion, and education for peace.
Giacomoâs story had already been told in 2024 by a podcast team at Vatican Radio â Vatican News in the five-part series Il talento di Giacomo. Il viaggio di un giovane poeta dalla disabilità allâispirazione (Giacomoâs Talent: The Journey of a Young Poet from Disability to Inspiration). Through poetry, music, and faith, the young man explained how difficulties and the loss of his brother Mattia had become sources of creativity, listening, and openness to others. The story foreshadowed the themes that Green Lava now brings to the screen.
A message capable of reaching far and wide
âI am truly happy and excited about this moment,â Giacomo says in a statement to Vatican Media, because Green Lava âhas reached a wider audience and will reach so many people.â At a time marked by âgreat uncertainty and global tensions,â the film can, in the young manâs view, be âa key to seeing the best that exists within each of us.â
The prospect of entering the Oscar race, he emphasizes, is not so much a source of personal pride as an opportunity âfor the message to reach as many people as possible.â Giacomo then recalls the support the Dicastery for Communication has given and recognizes an echo of Pope Francisâ appeal for fraternity, community, and care for creation in the film. âI am especially happy about this, because Pope Francisâ legacy must not be lost; on the contrary, it must be carried forward,â he says.
Having an illness is still a difficult trial, but it can also provide a different way of looking at reality. âIf you look at illness from another perspective, you understand many things about the way the world works, about suffering, and even about its meaning, which is sometimes not easy to understand,â Giacomo shares. And yet, he observes, people have a remarkable ability to keep moving forward, much like nature, which continually reclaims its space.
A story of faith and community
Lia Beltrami, the filmâs director, also shared with Vatican Media what this moment means: âTelling Giacomoâs story was a great challenge. His strength, his joy in living, and the depth of his being touch every cell in your body.â For her

items.title: New Holy See Permanent Observer to UN: Hate speech is not freedom of expression
items.summary: Archbishop Christophe Z. El Kassis delivers his first speech as the new Permanent Observer of the Holy See to the United Nations in New York on the importance of eliminating hate speech as it “poisons public discourse, inflames division, and too often prepares the ground for violence and persecution.” Read all
items.body_text:
New Holy See Permanent Observer to UN: Hate speech is not freedom of expression
Vatican News
The new Permanent Observer of the Holy See to the United Nations, Archbishop Christophe Z. El Kassis, presented his letter of appointment to the UN Secretary-General António Guterres on 16 September.
A day later, on 17 September, Archbishop El Kassis gave his first address at the Global Conference on Promoting Interreligious and Intercultural Dialogue and Tolerance in Countering Hate Speech in New York.
Addressing the Chair, the Archbishop reiterated the Holy Seeâs position that each and every individual is made in the image and likeness of God and has an inalienable dignity that cannot be lessened by any expression or ideology of hatred.
He stressed that âfrom this foundational truth flows the moral imperative to reject every form of intolerance, discrimination, and hate speech that wounds the human family and undermines the conditions for peaceful coexistence.â
Any hate speechâdirected at either individuals or communities because of their religion, race, nationality, or any other characteristicâgoes against the commandment to love oneâs neighbor. Moreover, it âpoisons public discourse, inflames division, and too often prepares the ground for violence and persecution.â
Archbishop El Kassis turned to the words of Pope Leo XIV in his Encyclical Letter Magnifica Humanitas: âThe first contribution we can make toward a more humane civilization is to be mindful of our words.â Words have great power. The first step in weaving âthe fabric of social peace and foster a culture of dialogue, tolerance and respect for differencesâ is taken when we disarm our words.
Yet, the new Permanent Observer argued that words are not enought to build peace. Authentic tolerance does not equal indifference or relativism. Rather, it means actively acknowledging each individualâs dignity and their own freedom of conscience. Patience in achieving dialogue, mutual understanding, and rejecting stereotypes is essential to true tolerance.
âIn this spirit the Holy See promotes interreligious and intercultural dialogue as an essential path toward overcoming prejudice and building a better world for all,â Archbishop El Kassis explained.
A fundamental right
âFreedom of expression is a fundamental right that must be protected,â the Archbishop stressed. However, this freedom comes with responsibilities.
Any words or speech that intentionally provoke violence or hatred cannot âclaim the protection of liberty; rather it erodes the very conditions in which genuine freedom can flourish.â
As the Popeâs encyclical urges, we must âdisarm communication of all prejudice and resentment, fanaticism and even hatred; let us free it from aggression. We do not need loud, forceful communication, but rather communication that is capable of listening and of gathering the voices of the weak who have no voice. Let us disarm words and we will help to disarm the world. Disarmed and disarming communication allows us to share a different view of the world and to act in a manner consistent with our human dignity.â
About Archbishop El Kassis
Born on 24 August 1968 in Beirut, Lebanon, Archbishop Christophe-Zakhia El-Kassis was ordained a priest of the Archeparchy of Beirut of the Maronites on 21 May 1994. Six years later, he joined the Diplomatic Service of the Holy See and has been worked at the Pontifical Representations in Indonesia, Sudan, and Türkiye.
In 2018, he was appointed Apostolic Nuncio to Pakistan and on 19 January 2019, he received the episcopal consecration from Cardinal Pietro Parolin in St. Peter's Basilica.
On 25 July 2026, Pope Leo XIV appointed Archbishop El-Kassis as Permanent Observer of the Holy See to the United Nations in New York.
